claims.text: Applying approximately 8–10% cold rolling followed by brief annealing at about 0.3–0.5 Tm will induce recrystallization in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The proposed treatment can induce recrystallization without appreciable grain coarsening or phase decomposition.
The proposed treatment will produce a finer and more homogeneous grain-size distribution in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Microstructural refinement will increase grain-boundary density.
Increased grain-boundary density will promote homogeneous plastic deformation.
Grain boundaries created by refinement will impede dislocation motion.
The refined microstructure will promote more uniform strain hardening.
More uniform strain hardening will delay localized necking under tensile loading.
Conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of 786 MPa.
Conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The reported 13.5% terminal strain is a tensile baseline that can be used as the baseline for uniform elongation.
Conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has limited tensile ductility and poor load-bearing reliability.
Processed HfZrTiTa0.53 will reach approximately 20% or greater uniform tensile elongation at room temperature.
The treatment will improve tensile elongation by approximately 50% or more relative to the stated 13.5% baseline.
The treatment will limit any yield-strength decrease to no more than approximately 10%.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has impact-triggered chemical-energy-release behavior that should be preserved by the treatment.
Grain refinement will not alter the mechanism responsible for chemical energy release during high-velocity impact.
The tensile prediction is intended to apply at room temperature under quasi-static loading at approximately 1×10^-3 s^-1.
Matched as-cast and treated specimens will be evaluated using tension, quasi-static compression, and high-velocity thin-steel-target impact tests.
Failure to reach about 20% uniform elongation while retaining yield strength within ±10% of baseline and comparable impact energy release will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% baseline is described as terminal or total tensile strain but is used as though it were a measured uniform elongation. Terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct tensile metrics, so the proposed before–after comparison is not matched.
The mechanism says refinement will improve ductility without reducing strength, whereas the predicted outcome explicitly allows a yield-strength reduction of up to about 10%.

The prediction limits only yield-strength loss to 10%, while the falsification rule requires strength to remain within ±10%. Thus, a strength increase greater than 10% is compatible with the prediction but would fail the stated falsification criterion.
